tier_reason: README benchstat table (purego vs avx2, n=10, 14th Gen Intel Core i9-14900) from the repo's own benchmarks in generated_test.go (BenchmarkAsm*/BenchmarkGo*, inputs from helpers_test.go randomBuffer); CPU is stated but the Go toolchain version is not, so it falls short of A and stays first-party C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README benchstat table (i9-14900, n=10, re-measured in the 2025-10-03 bugfix commit cb1b7b5), purego vs avx2 sec/op: VectorEquals8 145594.5ns -> 628.0ns (-99.57%, about 232x derived from page data); VectorEquals16 151.078us -> 1.325us (-99.12%); VectorEquals32 146.441us -> 2.626us (-98.21%); VectorEquals64 146.577us -> 4.468us (-96.95%); VectorGreaterThan8 146456.5ns -> 856.9ns (-99.41%); geomean over all 38 rows 133.0us -> 2.492us (-98.13%, about 53x derived from page data). The IsNaN rows, where the scalar branch is predictable, show only 23.555us -> 2.228us (float32, about 10.6x derived from page data) and 23.687us -> 4.410us (float64, about 5.4x derived from page data).
corrections.workload: comparison of one search value against 65,536 + rand(0..2047) elements of uint8/16/32/64 or float32/64 (Equals, NotEquals, GreaterThan, LessThan, GreaterEquals, LesserEquals, IsNaN) producing a bit-packed result mask with AVX2 VPCMP (AVX1 fallback); test data is drawn from three values ('a', 'b', 'c'; search 'b') plus 20 max-value or NaN entries
corrections.compiler_and_flags: go test -bench compared with benchstat (n=10, p=0.000); purego column is the scalar Go fallback (purego build tag), avx2 column the default amd64 build with runtime AVX2+BMI2 dispatch; GOMAXPROCS 32 (-32 suffix); Go toolchain version not stated (go.mod says go 1.18)
corrections.caveats: The baseline is the library's own naive scalar Go loop (gc compiler, no auto-vectorisation) with a data-dependent branch and a read-modify-write of the output byte per element. The test data matches the search value about one time in three at random, so that branch mispredicts heavily: the scalar Equals8 row costs about 2.2 ns per element, while the IsNaN rows (20 NaNs, predictable branch) cost about 0.35 ns per element and give only 10.6x (float32) and 5.4x (float64) (derived from page data). The 97-99.6% reductions therefore mostly measure branch mispredictions, not SIMD versus good (branchless or SWAR) scalar code, and there is no C/C++ -O3 baseline. The assembly is generated by internal/avo (asm_amd64.s and dispatch_amd64.go say 'Code generated by avo.go. DO NOT EDIT.'), with instructions chosen by hand in the avo DSL. The README table was re-measured in commit cb1b7b5 (2025-10-03, 'Bugfix: we accidentally did signed comparisons instead of unsigned'), so it postdates that correctness fix; two later optimisation commits (2025-10-04/05) are not reflected. README row names (VectorEquals8-32) do not match the current benchmark functions (BenchmarkAsmVectorEquals8 and BenchmarkGoVectorEquals8), so the table came from renamed or restructured runs. Buffer length is random per run (up to 3% different between columns). The Go Reference badge points at github.com/Jille/vectorcmp, a 0-star fork of this repo; the module path in go.mod is github.com/hexon/vectorcmp. amd64 only; other architectures use the scalar loop.

notes: Numbers match the README exactly; tier C stands. Main shortcoming for the orchestrator: the baseline is a branchy scalar Go loop on data that defeats branch prediction, so the 232x headline overstates the SIMD gain (predictable-branch IsNaN rows give 5.4-10.6x); Go version unstated; asm is avo-generated; last commit 2025-10-05 is just over 12 months old, so 'stale' is right.

tier_reason: First-party benchcmp table in the README, unchanged since the 2020-06-14 commit, with CPU and Go version unstated; the committed BenchmarkDecode calls encoding/hex's hex.Decode, so the decode 'new' column is not reproducible from the repo as committed. Tier stays C, but the decode claim is overstated because the SIMD decode path skips validation.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README 'typical results' (benchcmp output carried over unchanged from the 2020-06-14 commit; CPU and Go version not stated; GOMAXPROCS 8): Encode/16 30.7 -> 5.86 ns/op (5.25x), Encode/24 43.4 -> 17.8 ns/op (2.44x), Encode/1024 1793 -> 62.8 ns/op (571.10 -> 16298.50 MB/s, 28.54x); Decode/32 59.8 -> 10.4 ns/op (5.75x), Decode/48 87.5 -> 35.3 ns/op (2.48x), Decode/2048 3634 -> 182 ns/op (563.56 -> 11227.56 MB/s, 19.92x). The decode ratios compare a SIMD path that does no hex-digit validation against encoding/hex, which validates every byte, and they predate the table-driven stdlib decoder.
corrections.workload: hex encode of 16, 24 and 1024 bytes and hex decode of 32, 48 and 2048 characters, each built from a repeated fixed 8-byte pattern (valid input only)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: go test -bench with default settings ('Measured with project benchmarks under default settings'), old/new compared with benchcmp; Go version not stated (go.mod says go 1.14; numbers date from June 2020); no flags
corrections.caveats: The AVX2 decode kernel (decodeAVX2 in xhex_amd64.s) maps each character arithmetically ((c & 0x0f) + 9*(c >> 6)) with no range check, so an invalid hex byte inside any full 32-character block decodes to a wrong byte and Decode returns nil instead of InvalidByteError; only the scalar tail validates. This contradicts the README's 'API-compatible behavior with Go's encoding/hex', and TestDecodeErr only uses inputs shorter than 32 characters, so the gap is untested. The decode speedups therefore compare non-equivalent work. The committed BenchmarkDecode calls hex.Decode (stdlib) in both the 2020 and the current version, so the 'new' decode column needed an uncommitted edit; there is no side-by-side benchmark. The table is unchanged since 2020-06-14 (CPU, Go version unstated) and the asm has only had whitespace and comment edits since; current encoding/hex decodes with a lookup table and is several times faster than in 2020 (an independent go-simd/hex run recorded for tmthrgd/go-hex measured stdlib decode near 2.1 GB/s), so the decode ratios are stale. The decode kernel uses 128-bit X registers despite the AVX2 dispatch. The algorithm is credited to zbjornson/fast-hex (already listed in wave 7; xhex_amd64.go carries a 2017 Zach Bjornson copyright line), so this is a Go assembly port of that project. LICENSE is MIT but every source file header says Apache-2.0 (both OSI). amd64 with AVX2 only; elsewhere it is a scalar loop like encoding/hex. The 2026-04-02 commits only touched comments, docs and CI. Another Go SIMD hex package (tmthrgd/go-hex) is catalogued separately.

notes: Numbers match the README, but the SIMD decode path skips validation (invalid bytes silently accepted in 32-char blocks), the committed decode benchmark times the stdlib, and the 2020 numbers are stale against today's table-driven encoding/hex; tier C kept, claim corrected. Possible duplicate: xhex is a Go asm port of zbjornson/fast-hex (wave 7, credited in xhex_amd64.go); per the Go-port precedent (goant, go-quickjs) the orchestrator may record decision duplicate. License conflict: MIT LICENSE file vs Apache-2.0 file headers.
